claim: The composition of gut-associated microbial communities changes during intestinal inflammation, including an expansion of Enterobacteriaceae populations.
source: The composition of gut-associated microbial communities changes during intestinal inflammation, including an expansion of Enterobacteriaceae populations.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The bacterial genomes in the inflamed murine gut contained more genes encoding predicted hydrogen-utilizing hydrogenases compared to communities found under non-inflamed conditions.
source: The bacterial genomes in the inflamed murine gut and in patients with inflammatory bowel disease contained more genes encoding predicted hydrogen-utilizing hydrogenases compared to communities found under non-inflamed conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by metagenomic analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The bacterial genomes in patients with inflammatory bowel disease contained more genes encoding predicted hydrogen-utilizing hydrogenases compared to communities found under non-inflamed conditions.
source: The bacterial genomes in the inflamed murine gut and in patients with inflammatory bowel disease contained more genes encoding predicted hydrogen-utilizing hydrogenases compared to communities found under non-inflamed conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by metagenomic analysis shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: E. coli mutants lacking hydrogenase-1 and hydrogenase-2 displayed decreased fitness during colonization of the inflamed cecum.
source: E. coli mutants lacking hydrogenase-1 and hydrogenase-2 displayed decreased fitness during colonization of the inflamed cecum and colon.
evidence: This claim is supported by competitive colonization experiments shown in Figures 2C-D.

claim: E. coli mutants lacking hydrogenase-1 and hydrogenase-2 displayed decreased fitness during colonization of the inflamed colon.
source: E. coli mutants lacking hydrogenase-1 and hydrogenase-2 displayed decreased fitness during colonization of the inflamed cecum and colon.
evidence: This claim is supported by competitive colonization experiments shown in Figures 2C-D.

claim: Utilization of molecular hydrogen was in part dependent on respiration of inflammation-derived electron acceptors.
source: Utilization of molecular hydrogen was in part dependent on respiration of inflammation-derived electron acceptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments shown in Figure 7 demonstrating that H2 utilization requires fumarate reductase, cytochrome bd-II oxidase, or nitrate reductase activity.

claim: Under homeostatic conditions, the gut microbiota is dominated by obligate anaerobic bacteria in the Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes phyla.
source: Under homeostatic conditions, the gut microbiota is dominated by obligate anaerobic bacteria in the Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes phyla (Eckburg, 2005; Moore and Holdeman, 1974).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Eckburg, 2005 and Moore and Holdeman, 1974.

claim: Members of the phyla Actinobacteria, Verrucomicrobia, and Proteobacteria constitute minor populations in the healthy gut microbiota.
source: Members of the phyla Actinobacteria, Verrucomicrobia, and Proteobacteria constitute minor populations in the healthy gut microbiota.
evidence: This is a statement about the composition of the healthy gut microbiota, supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: During intestinal inflammation, microbial diversity decreases.
source: During intestinal inflammation, the composition of the gut microbiota changes compared to the homeostatic state. Microbial diversity decreases (Manichanh, 2006; Mirsepasi-Lauridsen, 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Manichanh, 2006 and Mirsepasi-Lauridsen, 2018.

claim: During intestinal inflammation, the prevalence of mucolytic bacteria in the mucosa increases.
source: the prevalence of mucolytic bacteria in the mucosa increases (Png, 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Png, 2010.

claim: During intestinal inflammation, populations of Enterobacteriaceae family members expand.
source: populations of Enterobacteriaceae family members expand (Haberman, 2014; Kotlowski, 2007; Lupp, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Haberman, 2014; Kotlowski, 2007; and Lupp, 2007.

claim: Disease-associated changes in gut microbiota composition have been observed in patients with inflammatory bowel disease.
source: Disease-associated changes in gut microbiota composition have been observed in patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) (Frank, 2007; Kotlowski, 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Frank, 2007 and Kotlowski, 2007.

claim: Disease-associated changes in gut microbiota composition have been observed in enteric pathogen infection.
source: enteric pathogen infection (Lupp, 2007; Stecher et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lupp, 2007; Stecher et al., 2007; and Wang et al., 2019.

claim: Disease-associated changes in gut microbiota composition have been observed in necrotizing enterocolitis.
source: necrotizing enterocolitis (Mai et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mai et al., 2011.

claim: Disease-associated changes in gut microbiota composition have been observed in animal models of colitis.
source: in animal models of colitis (Garrett, 2007; Lupp, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Garrett, 2007 and Lupp, 2007.

claim: Mucosal host responses contribute to microbiota changes.
source: Experiments in animal models suggest that mucosal host responses contribute to microbiota changes (Winter and Bäumler, 2014; Winter, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Winter and Bäumler, 2014 and Winter, 2013.

claim: Microbial communities can instigate or perpetuate disease in the context of genetic susceptibility.
source: microbial communities can instigate or perpetuate disease in the context of genetic susceptibility (Garrett, 2010; Manichanh, 2012; Zhu, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Garrett, 2010; Manichanh, 2012; and Zhu, 2018.

claim: In IBD patients, disease-associated changes in the microbiota composition, genetic coding capacity, and fecal metabolite concentrations correlate.
source: In IBD patients, disease-associated changes in the microbiota composition, genetic coding capacity, and fecal metabolite concentrations not only correlate (Franzosa, 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Franzosa, 2019.

claim: The availability of certain metabolites impacts microbial community structure.
source: the availability of certain metabolites impacts microbial community structure (Fornelos, 2020; Hughes, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fornelos, 2020 and Hughes, 2017.

claim: The inflammatory response produces reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, which when degraded in the gut lumen produce the electron acceptors tetrathionate, nitrate, and oxygen.
source: The inflammatory response produces reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, which when degraded in the gut lumen produce the electron acceptors tetrathionate, nitrate, and oxygen (Chanin, 2020; Winter, 2010; Winter, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chanin, 2020; Winter, 2010; and Winter, 2013.

claim: Changes in colonocyte metabolism during inflammation result in an increased availability of the electron acceptor oxygen.
source: Additionally, changes in colonocyte metabolism during inflammation also result in an increased availability of the electron acceptor oxygen (Cevallos, 2019; Hughes, 2017; Litvak, 2019; Lopez, 2016; Rivera-Chavez, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cevallos, 2019; Hughes, 2017; Litvak, 2019; Lopez, 2016; and Rivera-Chavez, 2016.

claim: The metabolic versatility of Enterobacteriaceae, particularly the ability to utilize a large repertoire of terminal electron acceptors, allows Enterobacteriaceae family members to thrive in the inflamed gut.
source: Findings from murine models of colitis suggest that the metabolic versatility of Enterobacteriaceae, particularly the ability to utilize a large repertoire of terminal electron acceptors, allows Enterobacteriaceae family members to thrive in the inflamed gut.
evidence: This claim is based on findings from murine models of colitis, representing an inference from experimental data.

claim: A functioning electron transport chain enables utilization of poorly accessible carbon sources.
source: A functioning electron transport chain also enables utilization of poorly accessible carbon sources (Faber et al., 2017; Fornelos, 2020; Price-Carter, 2001; Spiga and Winter, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Faber et al., 2017; Fornelos, 2020; Price-Carter, 2001; and Spiga and Winter, 2019.

claim: Formate dehydrogenases contribute to the expansion of Enterobacteriaceae in murine models of IBD.
source: Formate dehydrogenases contribute to the expansion of Enterobacteriaceae in murine models of IBD (Hughes, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hughes, 2017.

claim: Hydrogenases are a diverse family of metalloenzymes that catalyze the oxidation and/or production of molecular hydrogen.
source: Hydrogenases are a diverse family of metalloenzymes that catalyze the oxidation and/or production of molecular hydrogen (Benoit et al., 2020; Pinske and Sawers, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Benoit et al., 2020 and Pinske and Sawers, 2016.

claim: Hydrogenases are typically classified based on the metal content of the active site and their biochemical activity.
source: These enzymes are typically classified based on the metal content of the active site and their biochemical activity (Peters, 1998; Shima, 2008; Anne, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Peters, 1998; Shima, 2008; and Anne, 1995.

claim: The active site of [NiFe]-hydrogenases contains nickel and iron.
source: The active site of [NiFe]-hydrogenases contains nickel and iron
evidence: This is a statement about the composition of [NiFe]-hydrogenases, supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: The active site of [Fe]-hydrogenases includes one iron atom.
source: while the active site of [Fe]-hydrogenases and [FeFe]-hydrogenases includes one or two iron atoms, respectively.
evidence: This is a statement about the composition of [Fe]-hydrogenases, supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: The active site of [FeFe]-hydrogenases includes two iron atoms.
source: while the active site of [Fe]-hydrogenases and [FeFe]-hydrogenases includes one or two iron atoms, respectively.
evidence: This is a statement about the composition of [FeFe]-hydrogenases, supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Based on their activity, hydrogenases can be categorized into uptake, evolving, bidirectional, bifurcating, and sensory enzymes.
source: Based on their activity, hydrogenases can be further categorized into uptake, evolving, bidirectional, bifurcating, and sensory enzymes (Greening, 2016; Vignais and Billoud, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Greening, 2016 and Vignais and Billoud, 2007.

claim: Uptake hydrogenases convert H2 to two protons and two electrons, with the two electrons often participating in an electron transport chain.
source: Uptake hydrogenases convert H2 to two protons and two electrons, with the two electrons often participating in an electron transport chain.
evidence: This is a statement about the function of uptake hydrogenases, supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Hydrogenases defined as evolving are responsible for production of H2.
source: Conversely, hydrogenases defined as evolving are responsible for production of H2.
evidence: This is a statement about the function of evolving hydrogenases, supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Bidirectional hydrogenases can produce or oxidize H2.
source: Bidirectional hydrogenases can produce or oxidize H2 (reviewed in Tamagnini, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tamagnini, 2007.

claim: Bifurcating hydrogenases use an exergonic reaction (e.g., oxidation of ferredoxin) to drive an endergonic reaction (e.g., oxidation of NADH) without an ion gradient.
source: Bifurcating hydrogenases are enzymes involved in H2 metabolism that use an exergonic reaction (e.g., oxidation of ferredoxin) to drive an endergonic reaction (e.g., oxidation of NADH) without an ion gradient (Li, 2008; Schut and Adams, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li, 2008 and Schut and Adams, 2009.

claim: The genomes of many anaerobes encode predicted bifurcating hydrogenases.
source: Electron bifurcation was only recently demonstrated, yet the genomes of many anaerobes encode predicted bifurcating hydrogenases (Greening, 2016; Schut and Adams, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Greening, 2016 and Schut and Adams, 2009.

claim: Sensory hydrogenases detect changes in H2 partial pressure and then activate regulatory cascades controlling expression of additional hydrogenases.
source: Sensory hydrogenases detect changes in H2 partial pressure and then activate regulatory cascades controlling expression of additional hydrogenases (Lenz and Friedrich, 1998)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lenz and Friedrich, 1998.

claim: Many putative sensory hydrogenases are present in obligate anaerobes.
source: but additional study is required to characterize the many putative sensory hydrogenases present in obligate anaerobes (Greening, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Greening, 2016.

claim: Reads aligned to predicted uptake hydrogenases had a significantly higher abundance in DSS-treated mice than in mock-treated mice (p<0.05).
source: Notably, reads aligned to predicted uptake hydrogenases, enzymes responsible for oxidation of H2 via respiration, had a significantly higher abundance in DSS-treated mice than in mock-treated mice (p<0.05) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by metagenomic analysis data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: There was a significantly higher abundance of predicted uptake hydrogenases in patients with Crohn's disease than non-IBD controls (p<0.001).
source: Mirroring our observations in the murine model of colitis, we detected a significantly higher abundance of predicted uptake hydrogenases in patients with IBD than non-IBD controls (p<0.001 for patients with Crohn's disease; p<0.01 for patients with ulcerative colitis; Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by metagenomic analysis data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There was a significantly higher abundance of predicted uptake hydrogenases in patients with ulcerative colitis than non-IBD controls (p<0.01).
source: Mirroring our observations in the murine model of colitis, we detected a significantly higher abundance of predicted uptake hydrogenases in patients with IBD than non-IBD controls (p<0.001 for patients with Crohn's disease; p<0.01 for patients with ulcerative colitis; Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by metagenomic analysis data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There was a significantly higher abundance of reads that aligned to predicted evolving hydrogenases in IBD samples.
source: In contrast with our findings in the murine gut (Figure 1A), there was a significantly higher abundance of reads that aligned to predicted evolving hydrogenases in IBD samples (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by metagenomic analysis data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: The E. coli K-12 genome encodes four hydrogenases: two H2-oxidizing enzymes, hydrogenase-1 (Hyd-1) and hydrogenase-2 (Hyd-2), and two H2-evolving enzymes (hydrogenase-3 and hydrogenase-4).
source: The E. coli K-12 genome encodes four hydrogenases: two H2-oxidizing enzymes, hydrogenase-1 (Hyd-1) and hydrogenase-2 (Hyd-2), and two H2-evolving enzymes (hydrogenase-3 and hydrogenase-4).
evidence: This is a statement about the genomic content of E. coli K-12, supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Hyd-1 and Hyd-2 are encoded by the hya and hyb operons, respectively.
source: Hyd-1 and Hyd-2 are encoded by the hya and hyb operons, respectively (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the schematic representation in Figure 2A and established scientific knowledge.

claim: Inactivation of Hyd-1 and Hyd-2 activity had no discernible effect on growth of EcN under standard, aerobic laboratory conditions.
source: As expected, inactivation of Hyd-1 and Hyd-2 activity had no discernible effect on growth of EcN under standard, aerobic laboratory conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: H2 utilization only provided a growth advantage when an external electron acceptor, such as fumarate, was added to the media.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Yamamoto and Ishimoto, 1978), H2 utilization only provided a growth advantage when an external electron acceptor, such as fumarate, was added to the media.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro competition experiments and citation to Yamamoto and Ishimoto, 1978.

claim: The Hyd-2 enzyme is primarily responsible for enhancing growth under anaerobic culture conditions with H2 and fumarate.
source: The Hyd-2 enzyme is primarily responsible for enhancing growth under these culture conditions since a mutant lacking both Hyd-1 and Hyd-2 (Δhya Δhyb) was outcompeted by a strain only lacking Hyd-1 (Δhya); conversely, a Δhyb and a Δhya Δhyb mutant were equally fit in this assay (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro competition data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The EcN wild-type strain outcompeted the Δhya Δhyb mutant in the colonic content (12-fold).
source: The EcN wild-type strain outcompeted the Δhya Δhyb mutant in the colonic and cecal content (12-fold in the colon and 5.8-fold in the cecum; Figure 2C)
evidence: This claim is supported by competitive colonization data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The EcN wild-type strain outcompeted the Δhya Δhyb mutant in the cecal content (5.8-fold).
source: The EcN wild-type strain outcompeted the Δhya Δhyb mutant in the colonic and cecal content (12-fold in the colon and 5.8-fold in the cecum; Figure 2C)
evidence: This claim is supported by competitive colonization data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The MP1 wild-type strain was recovered in significantly higher numbers than the uptake hydrogenase-deficient mutant in the colonic content (25-fold).
source: while the MP1 wild-type strain was recovered in significantly higher numbers than the uptake hydrogenase-deficient mutant in the colonic and cecal content (25-fold and 22-fold, respectively; Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by competitive colonization data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The MP1 wild-type strain was recovered in significantly higher numbers than the uptake hydrogenase-deficient mutant in the cecal content (22-fold).
source: while the MP1 wild-type strain was recovered in significantly higher numbers than the uptake hydrogenase-deficient mutant in the colonic and cecal content (25-fold and 22-fold, respectively; Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by competitive colonization data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The wild-type strain was more abundant in the colonic content than the uptake hydrogenase-deficient mutant (4.7-fold).
source: Consistent with our observations in the competitive colonization experiments, the wild-type strain was more abundant in the colonic and cecal content than the uptake hydrogenase-deficient mutant (4.7-fold and 5.1-fold, respectively; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by single colonization data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The wild-type strain was more abundant in the cecal content than the uptake hydrogenase-deficient mutant (5.1-fold).
source: Consistent with our observations in the competitive colonization experiments, the wild-type strain was more abundant in the colonic and cecal content than the uptake hydrogenase-deficient mutant (4.7-fold and 5.1-fold, respectively; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by single colonization data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: H2 utilization via Hyd-1 and Hyd-2 enhances fitness and contributes to E. coli colonization of the inflamed large intestine.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that H2 utilization via Hyd-1 and Hyd-2 enhances fitness and contributes to E. coli colonization of the inflamed large intestine.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the colonization experiments shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Under homeostatic conditions, the wild-type strain and the Δhya Δhyb mutant colonized the colon and cecum at low levels.
source: Under homeostatic conditions, the wild-type strain and the Δhya Δhyb mutant colonized the colon and cecum at low levels (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by colonization data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: The wild-type strain had a marked fitness advantage over the Δhya Δhyb mutant in the DSS-treated mice.
source: However, the wild-type strain had a marked fitness advantage over the Δhya Δhyb mutant in the DSS-treated mice (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by colonization data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: The magnitude of the phenotype conferred by H2 utilization in E. coli increased as inflammation developed and stayed constant at later time points.
source: At the same time as inflammation developed, the magnitude of the phenotype conferred by H2 utilization in E. coli increased and stayed constant at later time points (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course colonization data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Colon length was inversely correlated with the competitive fitness advantage of the wild-type strain over the Δhya Δhyb mutant.
source: Notably, colon length, a sensitive measure of colitis, was inversely correlated with the competitive fitness advantage of the wild-type strain over the Δhya Δhyb mutant (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: Hyd-1 and Hyd-2 provide a notable fitness advantage to E. coli during the inflammation-associated expansion of the Enterobacteriaceae population.
source: Taken together, we conclude that Hyd-1 and Hyd-2 provide a notable fitness advantage to E. coli during the inflammation-associated expansion of the Enterobacteriaceae population.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the colonization experiments shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The wild-type E. coli strains significantly outcompeted the Δhya Δhyb mutants in the piroxicam-accelerated Il10-/- colitis model, regardless of the experimental setting.
source: Importantly, the wild-type E. coli strains significantly outcompeted the Δhya Δhyb mutants, regardless of the experimental setting (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by colonization data shown in Figure 6C-E.

claim: H2 utilization provides a fitness advantage to E. coli in both chemically induced and genetically induced models of murine colitis.
source: Taken together, H2 utilization provides a fitness advantage to E. coli in both chemically induced and genetically induced models of murine colitis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the colonization experiments shown in Figures 2-6.

claim: Hyd-1 and Hyd-2 are both H2-utilizing, membrane-bound hydrogenases that transfer electrons from H2 oxidation to the electron transport chain.
source: Hyd-1 and Hyd-2 are both H2-utilizing, membrane-bound hydrogenases that transfer electrons from H2 oxidation to the electron transport chain.
evidence: This is a statement about the function of Hyd-1 and Hyd-2, supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: In vitro, hydrogen oxidation is coupled to fumarate reduction and nitrate respiration.
source: In vitro, hydrogen oxidation is coupled to fumarate reduction and nitrate respiration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; Laurinavichene and Tsygankov, 2001; Yamamoto and Ishimoto, 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and citations to Laurinavichene and Tsygankov, 2001 and Yamamoto and Ishimoto, 1978.

claim: Nitrate is the preferred electron acceptor for H2 utilization in E. coli.
source: The redox potential of the nitrate/nitrite couple is more favorable than that of fumarate/succinate. As such, nitrate is the preferred electron acceptor for H2 utilization in E. coli (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro competition data shown in Figure 7A and knowledge of redox potentials.

claim: During gut inflammation, levels of inducible nitric oxide synthase (Nos2) increase.
source: During gut inflammation, levels of inducible nitric oxide synthase (Nos2) increase (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C; Singer, 1996; Winter, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by mRNA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and citations to Singer, 1996 and Winter, 2013.

claim: Increased levels of inducible nitric oxide synthase enable nitrate respiration, which supports growth of Enterobacteriaceae family members.
source: During gut inflammation, levels of inducible nitric oxide synthase (Nos2) increase (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C; Singer, 1996; Winter, 2013) enabling nitrate respiration, which supports growth of Enterobacteriaceae family members (Hughes, 2017; Winter, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hughes, 2017 and Winter, 2013.

claim: E. coli respires oxygen using the cytochrome bd-II oxidase enzyme (AppBCX).
source: In addition, E. coli respires oxygen using the cytochrome bd-II oxidase enzyme (AppBCX) (Chanin, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chanin, 2020.

claim: The competitive advantage conferred by Hyd-1 and Hyd-2 was significantly reduced in the absence of fumarate reductase activity.
source: The competitive advantage conferred by Hyd-1 and Hyd-2 was significantly reduced in the absence of fumarate reductase, cytochrome bd-II oxidase, or nitrate reductase activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by colonization data shown in Figure 7B-C.

claim: The competitive advantage conferred by Hyd-1 and Hyd-2 was significantly reduced in the absence of cytochrome bd-II oxidase activity.
source: The competitive advantage conferred by Hyd-1 and Hyd-2 was significantly reduced in the absence of fumarate reductase, cytochrome bd-II oxidase, or nitrate reductase activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by colonization data shown in Figure 7B-C.

claim: The competitive advantage conferred by Hyd-1 and Hyd-2 was significantly reduced in the absence of nitrate reductase activity.
source: The competitive advantage conferred by Hyd-1 and Hyd-2 was significantly reduced in the absence of fumarate reductase, cytochrome bd-II oxidase, or nitrate reductase activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by colonization data shown in Figure 7B-C.

claim: Inactivation of each reductase did not completely abolish the H2 utilization phenotype.
source: Consistent with the idea that all three electron acceptors contribute to the H2 utilization phenotype, inactivation of each reductase did not completely abolish the phenotype (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by colonization data shown in Figure 7B-C.

claim: Hyd-1 and Hyd-2 are members of distinct [NiFe]-hydrogenase subgroups, differing in subunit composition and the range of redox potentials at which they function optimally.
source: Hyd-1 and Hyd-2 are members of distinct [NiFe]-hydrogenase subgroups, differing in subunit composition and the range of redox potentials at which they function optimally (Beaton et al., 2018; Greening, 2016; Lukey, 2010; Volbeda et al., 2013) (reviewed in Pinske and Sawers, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Beaton et al., 2018; Greening, 2016; Lukey, 2010; Volbeda et al., 2013; and Pinske and Sawers, 2016.

claim: The EcN wild-type strain outcompeted the Δhya mutant in the colonic content (3.3-fold).
source: In the DSS colitis model (Figure 8A), the EcN wild-type strain outcompeted the Δhya mutant in the colonic and cecal content (3.3-fold and 2.2-fold, respectively) (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by colonization data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The EcN wild-type strain outcompeted the Δhya mutant in the cecal content (2.2-fold).
source: In the DSS colitis model (Figure 8A), the EcN wild-type strain outcompeted the Δhya mutant in the colonic and cecal content (3.3-fold and 2.2-fold, respectively) (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by colonization data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The Δhyb mutant was recovered in significantly lower numbers than the EcN wild-type strain from colonic content (6.4-fold).
source: Similarly, the Δhyb mutant was recovered in significantly lower numbers than the EcN wild-type strain from both colonic and cecal content (6.4-fold and 4.7-fold, respectively; Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by colonization data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The Δhyb mutant was recovered in significantly lower numbers than the EcN wild-type strain from cecal content (4.7-fold).
source: Similarly, the Δhyb mutant was recovered in significantly lower numbers than the EcN wild-type strain from both colonic and cecal content (6.4-fold and 4.7-fold, respectively; Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by colonization data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Both Hyd-1 and Hyd-2 provide a fitness advantage for E. coli during colitis.
source: We thus conclude that both Hyd-1 and Hyd-2 provide a fitness advantage for E. coli during colitis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the colonization experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: H2 metabolism supports microbial respiration, fermentation, and carbon fixation.
source: H2 metabolism supports microbial respiration, fermentation, and carbon fixation (Vignais and Billoud, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vignais and Billoud, 2007.

claim: H2 metabolism is perturbed during murine non-infectious colitis and in human IBD patients.
source: Our data suggests that H2 metabolism is perturbed during murine non-infectious colitis and in human IBD patients.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the metagenomic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Animal models of colitis could be useful tools to probe the physiological role of H2 metabolism in the gut microbiota.
source: We propose that animal models of colitis could be useful tools to probe the physiological role of H2 metabolism in the gut microbiota.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the findings of the study.

claim: H2 is a key metabolite involved in cross-feeding between members of the gut microbiota.
source: H2 is a key metabolite involved in cross-feeding between members of the gut microbiota (reviewed in Smith, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Smith, 2019.

claim: H2 metabolism supports gut colonization of methanogens, acetogens, and sulfate-reducing bacteria.
source: H2 metabolism supports gut colonization of methanogens, acetogens, and sulfate-reducing bacteria (Bernalier, 1996; Rey, 2013; Ruaud et al., 2020; Samuel, 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bernalier, 1996; Rey, 2013; Ruaud et al., 2020; and Samuel, 2007.

claim: Methanogens, acetogens, and sulfate-reducing bacteria prevent the accumulation of a high H2 partial pressure that can inhibit polysaccharide fermentation.
source: and these microbes, in turn, prevent the accumulation of a high H2 partial pressure that can inhibit polysaccharide fermentation (Samuel and Gordon, 2006; Stams, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Samuel and Gordon, 2006 and Stams, 1994.

claim: The increased abundance of genes encoding uptake hydrogenases in microbial communities in the inflamed gut is consistent with an inflammation-disruption of H2 syntrophic networks.
source: The increased abundance of genes encoding uptake hydrogenases in microbial communities in the inflamed gut and the enhanced fitness advantage provided by H2 oxidation to E. coli in murine models of colitis are consistent with an inflammation-disruption of H2 syntrophic networks.
evidence: This is an inference based on the metagenomic and colonization data.

claim: C. difficile expands due to accumulation of the metabolite succinate via loss of microbial consumption.
source: Previous work with Clostridium difficile established that C. difficile expands due to accumulation of the metabolite succinate via loss of microbial consumption (Ferreyra, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ferreyra, 2014.

claim: The lack of succinate consumption by the microbiota occurs during antibiotic treatment, chemically induced motility disturbance, and impaired IL-22-mediated host glycosylation.
source: The lack of succinate consumption by the microbiota was shown to occur during antibiotic treatment, chemically induced motility disturbance, and impaired IL-22-mediated host glycosylation (Ferreyra, 2014; Nagao-Kitamoto, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ferreyra, 2014 and Nagao-Kitamoto, 2020.

claim: Changes in microbe-microbe H2 exchange during inflammation might allow E. coli to access a H2 pool.
source: It is conceivable that changes in microbe-microbe H2 exchange during inflammation might allow E. coli to access a H2 pool.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible mechanism.

claim: In the inflamed intestine, H2 utilization via Hyd-1 and Hyd-2 requires fumarate reductase, cytochrome bd-II oxidase, or nitrate reductase activity.
source: Here, we demonstrate that in the inflamed intestine, H2 utilization via Hyd-1 and Hyd-2 requires fumarate reductase, cytochrome bd-II oxidase, or nitrate reductase activity (Figure 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by colonization data shown in Figure 7 and summarized in Figure 9.

claim: Nitrate is generated as a by-product of reactive nitrogen species metabolism.
source: Nitrate is generated as a by-product of reactive nitrogen species metabolism
evidence: This is a statement about the generation of nitrate, supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Nitrate respiration contributes to the expansion of Enterobacteriaceae family members during flares.
source: and nitrate respiration contributes to the expansion of Enterobacteriaceae family members during flares (Hughes, 2017; Winter, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hughes, 2017 and Winter, 2013.

claim: Detoxification of inflammatory reactive oxygen species in the inflamed gut gives E. coli access to molecular oxygen and facilitates respiration via AppBCX.
source: Detoxification of inflammatory reactive oxygen species in the inflamed gut gives E. coli access to molecular oxygen and facilitates respiration via AppBCX (Chanin, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chanin, 2020.

claim: Hyd-1 is oxygen-tolerant.
source: Curiously, Hyd-1 is oxygen-tolerant (Lukey, 2011; Volbeda et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lukey, 2011 and Volbeda et al., 2012.

claim: Hyd-1 is induced under anaerobic conditions.
source: but induced under anaerobic conditions (Brøndsted and Atlung, 1994; Richard et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brøndsted and Atlung, 1994 and Richard et al., 1999.

claim: Bacterial nitrate respiration and AppBCX-dependent oxygen respiration are consequences of the host's inflammatory reactive oxygen and nitrogen metabolism.
source: The fact that bacterial nitrate respiration and AppBCX-dependent oxygen respiration are consequences of the host's inflammatory reactive oxygen and nitrogen metabolism may in part explain why H2 utilization contributes to the bloom of E. coli in mouse models of colitis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and established knowledge.

claim: The concentration of free fumarate is very low in the large intestine.
source: The concentration of free fumarate is very low in the large intestine, but fumarate can readily be generated from other sources such as aspartate or malate (Nguyen, 2020; Schubert et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nguyen, 2020 and Schubert et al., 2021.

claim: Fumarate can readily be generated from other sources such as aspartate or malate.
source: The concentration of free fumarate is very low in the large intestine, but fumarate can readily be generated from other sources such as aspartate or malate (Nguyen, 2020; Schubert et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nguyen, 2020 and Schubert et al., 2021.

claim: The three electron acceptors (fumarate, nitrate, oxygen) couple to Hyd-1 or Hyd-2 in different, spatially distinct, subpopulations or at different time points as inflammation develops.
source: This outcome is consistent with a scenario in which these three electron acceptors couple to Hyd-1 or Hyd-2 in different, spatially distinct, subpopulations or at different time points as inflammation develops.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: H2 uptake is important for STm virulence.
source: H2 uptake is important for STm virulence (Lamichhane-Khadka, 2015; Maier, 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lamichhane-Khadka, 2015 and Maier, 2004.

claim: H2 uptake facilitates STm gut colonization.
source: and it facilitates STm gut colonization (Maier et al., 2014; Maier, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Maier et al., 2014 and Maier, 2013.

claim: H2 uptake facilitates STm fecal shedding.
source: and fecal shedding (Lam and Monack, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lam and Monack, 2014.

claim: The role of hydrogenases with regards to STm systemic colonization has resulted in different outcomes, depending on the bacterial strain, route of inoculation, mouse background, and gut microbiota status.
source: The role of hydrogenases with regards to STm systemic colonization has resulted in different outcomes, depending on the bacterial strain, route of inoculation, mouse background, and gut microbiota status (Craig, 2013; Maier et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Craig, 2013 and Maier et al., 2014.

claim: H2 uptake contributes to gut colonization in a mouse and human commensal E. coli strain during non-infectious colitis.
source: In our study, we observed that H2 uptake contributes to gut colonization in a mouse and human commensal E. coli strain, and both Hyd-1 and Hyd-2 play a role in facilitating E. coli gut colonization during non-infectious colitis.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.
